question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2} \cdot y=\frac{3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}}{y^{4}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+6\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=- 3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\\ n&=-4.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{-4}$ and set $z=y^{5}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=5 \cdot y^{4}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- 15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\right)z=15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - 15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}\,z\right)=15 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{2} \cdot e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}z=- e^{- 5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}} - 1.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{5}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\sqrt[5]{C \cdot e^{5 \cdot \left(x+6\right)^{3}} - 1}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- \left(x-4\right)^{2} \cdot y=- \frac{\left(x-4\right)^{2}}{y^{4}}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x-4\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=- \left(x-4\right)^{2}\\ q(x)&=- \left(x-4\right)^{2}\\ n&=-4.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{-4}$ and set $z=y^{5}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=5 \cdot y^{4}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- 5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{2}\right)z=- 5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{2}.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - 5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}}\,z\right)=- 5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{2} \cdot e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}}z=e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}} + 1.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{5}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\sqrt[5]{C \cdot e^{\frac{5 \cdot \left(x-4\right)^{3}}{3}} + 1}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+3 \cdot y=2 \cdot \left(x-4\right) \cdot y^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x-4\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=3\\ q(x)&=2 \cdot \left(x-4\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-6\right)z=- 4 \cdot \left(x-4\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -6\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)}\,z\right)=- 4 \cdot \left(x-4\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)}z=\frac{2 \cdot \left(\left(x-4\right) + \frac{1}{6}\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)}}{3}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)} + \frac{2 \cdot \left(x-4\right)}{3} + \frac{1}{9}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{9}{9 \cdot C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x-4\right)} + 6 \cdot \left(x-4\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}- y=- 2 \cdot \sqrt{y}.
$$ Take $y>0$. For even powers and powers of $2/3$ in the choices, retain only intervals where the base is positive. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-1\\ q(x)&=-2\\ n&=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{2 \cdot \sqrt{y}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)z=-1.$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \frac{x}{2}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{x}{2}}\,z\right)=- e^{- \frac{x}{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \frac{x}{2}}z=2 \cdot e^{- \frac{x}{2}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{x}{2}} + 2.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(C \cdot e^{\frac{x}{2}} + 2\right)^{2}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. The displayed expression for $z$ must be positive because $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+3 \cdot \left(x+5\right) \cdot y=- 2 \cdot \left(x+5\right) \cdot y^{2}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x+5\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)\\ q(x)&=- 2 \cdot \left(x+5\right)\\ n&=2.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{2}$ and set $z=y^{-1}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{1}{y^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- 3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)\right)z=2 \cdot \left(x+5\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int - 3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}}\,z\right)=2 \cdot \left(x+5\right) \cdot e^{- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}}z=- \frac{2 \cdot e^{- \frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}}}{3}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}} - \frac{2}{3}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-1}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\frac{3}{3 \cdot C \cdot e^{\frac{3 \cdot \left(x+5\right)^{2}}{2}} - 2}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals.
